analysis.one_liner: Gives state and local government employees a federally guaranteed right to unionize and bargain collectively.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 191 cosponsors — 185 of 217 House Democrats and 6 of 223 House Republicans — and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no action on it since April 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill sets a federal floor for collective bargaining rights for state and local government employees, such as teachers, nurses, first responders, and transit workers. The Federal Labor Relations Authority would judge whether each state's laws give workers those rights; in states that fall short, the federal agency would run union elections, handle complaints, and enforce bargaining rules, while states that already meet the standard keep their own systems. The bill also bans strikes and lockouts by emergency and law-enforcement personnel when they would disrupt public safety services.
analysis.who_benefits: Public employees in states that do not currently guarantee union organizing and collective bargaining rights. They would gain a federal right to form a union, have it recognized through an election, bargain over wages, hours, and working conditions, get binding resolution of contract disputes, and sue to enforce those rights with possible attorneys' fees.

how_it_helps.text: Public and supervisory employees get a federal right to self-organize, form or join a labor organization, bargain collectively through representatives of their choosing, and act together for mutual aid or protection.

Public employers must recognize a union chosen by majority election or voluntary recognition, bargain with it, and put any agreement in writing; existing unions cannot be forced through recertification unless at least 30 percent of workers petition for it.
States must have an impasse-resolution mechanism — such as fact-finding, mediation, or arbitration — that culminates in a binding resolution when bargaining stalls.
Workers gain payroll deduction of union fees and a private right of action to sue a state administrator to enforce the law or agency orders, with attorneys' fees available.

States whose laws already meet the federal minimum keep their own systems untouched, and exceptions preserve existing arrangements for small towns, the National Guard, legislative approval of contracts, and pension bargaining.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, and ultimately their taxpayers, would bear the cost of bargaining obligations, written contracts, and binding resolution of contract disputes. States that currently allow workers no or limited bargaining rights would have their labor rules administered by a federal agency.

drawbacks.text: In states where voters and legislatures have chosen to limit or prohibit bargaining by government workers, a federal determination would override that state policy and put a federal agency in charge of the state's public-employer labor relations.
Binding resolution of bargaining impasses can lock in contract terms that state and local officials did not agree to, with the fiscal cost falling on government budgets and taxpayers.

The bill restricts strikes and other job actions by emergency-services employees and law enforcement officers when they would measurably disrupt public safety services, so some workers would gain bargaining duties without full strike leverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in states without bargaining rights, the bill offers a substantial, enforceable new right. The main costs are fiscal — binding contract outcomes for governments — and federalism: state labor policies, including ones adopted by referendum in some states, would be displaced wherever they fall short of the federal minimum. The bill softens this by leaving compliant state systems alone, carving out small towns and pensions, and using the state's own agency where possible.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in April 2025, and the committee has not scheduled it for a markup or any vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross introduced the bill on April 8, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
191 members cosponsored it — 185 of 217 House Democrats and 6 of 223 House Republicans.
The action history shows no further steps since the committee referral: no markup, no committee vote, no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, the status quo holds: state and local governments in states without bargaining mandates keep their current labor rules, and government workers in those states remain without federal bargaining rights.

sides.party_line_note: Support is nearly unanimous among Democrats (185 of 217) with token Republican support (6 of 223); the committee where the bill sits is controlled by House Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would let unions organize government workers in states that currently bar or limit it, secure payroll deduction of dues, and make unions the exclusive bargaining representatives. Union growth and worker bargaining rights rise together under this bill.

As the employers covered by the bill, state and local governments would face union recognition duties, written contracts, and binding impasse resolution, funded by their budgets. Their interest in keeping labor costs down runs against the bill's expansion of worker bargaining rights.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in a committee controlled by House Republicans, who have not taken it up. With no markup scheduled and a Congress that runs through early January 2027, the standard path for a bill at this stage with this level of committee inaction is to remain unreported and expire at the end of the Congress; it would need leadership to schedule committee or floor action to move.
